**Introduction:** Sleep duration is one of the most consequential modifiable health behaviors in childhood and adolescence, with insufficient sleep linked to adverse cognitive, emotional, and physical outcomes across development.[@owens_insufficient_2014] Tracking how sleep duration shifts across age groups requires large, representative samples measured with methods that scale beyond the laboratory. Consumer wearables let researchers measure sleep duration in daily life, across multiple nights, and in samples much larger than polysomnography or actigraphy can support. At the same time, they raise a measurement concern—sleep estimates come from proprietary algorithms that researchers cannot always inspect or rescore independently.

The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study[@karcher2021] illustrates this concern. ABCD includes Fitbit-derived sleep variables but does not provide the raw accelerometry data needed to apply pediatric scoring algorithms. Fitbit devices have been evaluated against polysomnography in adults[@dezambotti2018], but pediatric validation is sparser. We therefore compared ABCD Fitbit-derived sleep-duration distributions with published pediatric sleep-duration references to evaluate whether the estimates were plausible at the population level. Alignment with those benchmarks would support that the durations reflect how long children and adolescents in the United States are actually sleeping, not merely what a particular algorithm reports.

**Method:** Fitbit sleep data came from ABCD Study release 7.0. Participant-sessions were included if they had at least 5 valid weekdays and 2 valid weekend days, with weekend days defined as Saturday and Sunday based on the wake date. For each participant-session, we calculated mean sleep duration separately for valid weekdays and weekend days, then combined them into a weighted weekly estimate using ((5 × mean weekday) + (2 × mean weekend)) / 7 to mirror the distribution of weekdays and weekend days.

We estimated age-specific 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 90th percentiles of Fitbit-derived sleep duration in 0.5-year age bins. We compared these ABCD curves with six published benchmarks: two parent-report references from the Zurich Longitudinal Studies (ZLS)[@iglowstein2003] and the Panel Study of Income Dynamics Child Development Supplement (PSID-CDS)[@williams2013], three actigraphy-based references from National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES)[@freeman2026], the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study (FFCWS)[@ffcwsdaily2023], and the Pediatric Adenotonsillectomy Trial for Snoring (PATS)[@redline2023pats], and one meta-analytic pediatric prediction curve (based on 57 actigraphy studies)[@galland2018]. To describe rough agreement quantitatively, we also calculated the mean difference and range across overlapping ages, with negative values indicating shorter sleep duration in ABCD compared to the reference data.

**Results:** The analytic sample included `r fmt_int(n_participant_visits)` participant-visits from `r fmt_int(n_unique_youths)` unique youths. Mean age was `r fmt2(mean_age)` years (range, `r fmt2(min_age)` to `r fmt2(max_age)`). Mean weighted sleep duration was `r fmt2(mean_weighted_duration)` hours (*SD* = `r fmt2(sd_weighted_duration)`). Across age bins, the median values of the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentile curves were `r fmt2(median_p10)`, `r fmt2(median_p50)`, and `r fmt2(median_p90)` hours, respectively.

Figure 1 shows the ABCD Fitbit curves overlaid on each published reference. For the parent-report references, the ABCD curves followed a similar age-related pattern but ran systematically below them; mean differences were `r fmt2(diffs$iglowstein$mean)` hours for the ZLS (range, `r fmt_range(diffs$iglowstein$min, diffs$iglowstein$max)`) and `r fmt2(diffs$williams$mean)` hours for PSID-CDS (range, `r fmt_range(diffs$williams$min, diffs$williams$max)`). Agreement was closer for the actigraphy-based references, for which mean differences were `r fmt2(diffs$nhanes$mean)` hours for NHANES (range, `r fmt_range(diffs$nhanes$min, diffs$nhanes$max)`), `r fmt2(diffs$ffcws$mean)` hours for FFCWS (range, `r fmt_range(diffs$ffcws$min, diffs$ffcws$max)`), and `r fmt2(diffs$pats$mean)` hours for PATS (range, `r fmt_range(diffs$pats$min, diffs$pats$max)`). The mean difference from the meta-analytic prediction curve was `r fmt2(diffs$galland$mean)` hours (range, `r fmt_range(diffs$galland$min, diffs$galland$max)`).

**Discussion:** Compared with published pediatric sleep-duration references, ABCD Fitbit-derived estimates were systematically shorter than parent-report norms but close to objective actigraphy-based benchmarks. This pattern is consistent with prior evidence that, in ABCD and elsewhere, parent and youth reports tend to overestimate sleep duration relative to device-derived estimates.[@feldman2026]

Population-level alignment, however, is not the same as individual-level accuracy. Two scoring algorithms could yield very different per-night or per-person estimates and still produce similar age-conditional distributions, if systematic over- and underestimation cancel across the sample. Establishing whether any given Fitbit estimate is close to the truth requires paired comparisons in the ABCD Fitbit subsample against polysomnography or research-grade actigraphy. Despite these limitations, the close alignment with objectively measured pediatric sleep benchmarks increases our confidence in the validity of the Fitbit-derived estimates and their use in advancing pediatric sleep science.

## Figure

**Figure 1. Comparison of ABCD Fitbit Sleep Duration Distributions With Published Normative Data**

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(outputs_dir, "figure1.png"))
```

**Note.** Lines mark the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles of estimated sleep duration from each study, with shaded bands spanning the 25th–75th (darker) and 10th–90th (lighter) percentile ranges. Panels A and B show parent-report references from the ZLS[@iglowstein2003] and PSID-CDS[@williams2013], respectively. Panel C shows the meta-analytic best-fit prediction curve from Galland et al.[@galland2018]; circles indicate the individual studies sized proportionately to their weight in the meta-analysis. Panels D, E, and F show actigraphy-based references from NHANES[@freeman2026], FFCWS[@ffcwsdaily2023], and PATS[@redline2023pats], respectively. ABCD = Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study; FFCWS = Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study; NHANES = National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey; PATS = Pediatric Adenotonsillectomy Trial for Snoring; PSID-CDS = Panel Study of Income Dynamics Child Development Supplement; ZLS = Zurich Longitudinal Studies.
